market.title: Hard goods are compounding at ~7.4%; apparel and athleisure at 12%+

body.text: Sports and fitness goods: USD 5.24B in 2025 to USD 10.70B by 2035 at 7.4%. Athleisure in India: 12.7% CAGR 2026–33, well above the global 9.9%. The category PlayBlue leads with — curated equipment and specialist gear — grows at roughly half the rate of the category it competes in on price.

market.title: Value growth is outpacing volume as the mix premiumises

body.text: Technical materials, smart fitness systems and branded protective gear are lifting average realisation. Volume growth of 5.2–5.5% against 7.4% value growth. Globally, the premium athleisure segment is forecast at 10.45% CAGR against 65.6% of 2025 revenue still sitting in mass-market lines. Favourable for a curated premium format — provided Indian willingness to pay has moved as fast as the assortment.

market.title: Kids and women are the fastest-growing end-user segments

body.text: Globally the kids and children segment is forecast at 11.82% CAGR to 2031 against 91.8% of 2025 revenue coming from adults. In India, women were the largest athleisure segment at 56.8% of 2025 share and also the fastest growing — the insight BlissClub built a ₹131.5 Cr (FY25, audited) business on. Both segments are under-served by a format built around serious athletes.

market.title: Online is taking share of sports retail faster than stores

body.text: Sports and athletic goods stores held 39.7% of 2025 athleisure sales globally, but online retail is advancing at 11.36% CAGR. In India, Myntra, Amazon, Ajio and Decathlon reported over 35% YoY growth in online sports apparel demand in 2024, and online fashion order volume rose 20.9% in FY24. PlayBlue's parallel e-commerce build is strategically correct — and the stage it is least equipped for.

market.title: Price sensitivity and counterfeit supply remain the binding constraint

body.text: Strong price sensitivity and the continued dominance of unorganised and counterfeit channels are named as the primary restraint on the India sports apparel market, particularly in tier-II and tier-III cities. Over 70% of premium sportswear sold in India in 2024 came from international brands — a small, contested, metro-concentrated pool.

regulatory.title: Direct state support for domestic sports-goods manufacturing

body.text: An INR 500 crore sports-goods manufacturing allocation plus a proposed cluster-development roadmap is expected to redirect profit pools toward design, quality assurance, connected products, e-commerce fulfilment and compliant domestic production. This advantages players with local sourcing depth — Decathlon and the domestic manufacturers — over a multi-brand importer.

regulatory.title: Local sourcing has hardened from policy into competitive economics

body.text: Decathlon's shift from 68% to a targeted 85% local sourcing is framed around Make in India but functions as a cost and resilience advantage. For a retailer dependent on imported global brands, this widens the landed-cost gap on comparable products — and it is the strongest argument for PlayBlue eventually developing private label.

regulatory.title: Public sports investment is expanding the participation base

body.text: The Department of Sport budget grew from roughly $79M in 2011–12 to $211M in 2021–22. Sustained public and private infrastructure investment is cited across market analyses as a participation driver in both urban and rural areas. India's Olympic hosting ambition — a subject PlayBlue itself has published on — sits within this. Slow-moving but directionally favourable.

regulatory.title: FDI structure in multi-brand retail — flagged, not asserted

body.text: India's distinction between single-brand and multi-brand retail FDI has historically constrained foreign-owned multi-brand formats and shaped partnership structures. Relevant to how PlayBlue structures brand relationships and any future foreign strategic investment — particularly given a Japanese co-lead investor. We have not established the current position and would not put a figure on it without a specialist legal read.

capital.title: Dedicated sports-sector venture capital now exists at meaningful scale

body.text: Centre Court Capital closed a ₹410 crore maiden fund in December 2025, oversubscribed against a ₹350 crore target. Cheques of ₹8–24 crore across 15–18 companies in sports, fitness, wellness and social gaming, with 30–40% reserved for follow-ons and deployment expected within 12–18 months. Sector-specific capital at this scale did not exist in India three years ago.

capital.title: Athlete and operator capital is entering the LP base

body.text: Centre Court's fund drew Neeraj Chopra, Rishabh Pant, PV Sindhu and Jemimah Rodrigues alongside Binny Bansal, Mithun Sacheti and Ankit Nagori, with institutional backing from Premji Invest and SIDBI. Athlete-adjacent capital brings distribution and credibility, not only money — directly relevant to PlayBlue's brand-access advantage.

capital.title: The capital is going to infrastructure and analytics, not merchandising

body.text: Centre Court's portfolio spans sports infrastructure (Michezo Sports, ~USD 2.5M pre-Series A with Zerodha's Rainmatter), broadcast technology (Quidich Innovation Labs) and sports data (Stupa). The stated thesis names infrastructure, analytics and fan-facing products. A data-led retailer fits that thesis; a purely merchandising one fits it less well.

capital.title: Homegrown sports brands are attracting institutional growth capital

body.text: Technosport is reported to have raised ₹175 Cr from A91 Partners, though also reported elsewhere as $25M — unverified pending MCA/Tracxn confirmation. BlissClub has raised over $21M from Elevation Capital and Eight Roads and is raising a further $25M, against an audited FY25 revenue of ₹131.5 Cr (RoC filing via Entrackr). Capital is validating vertical integration and category focus — the opposite structural bet to multi-brand curation. Worth understanding how PlayBlue's Series A story differentiates from theirs.

capital.title: Cross-border strategic capital is entering Indian sport

body.text: MIXI Global Investments co-leading PlayBlue's seed round is an instance of Japanese strategic capital taking positions in Indian sports consumer businesses. Suggests the category is being underwritten internationally, which matters for Series A optionality and for who the eventual acquirers might be.

realEstate.title: Retail leasing hit a post-COVID high in 2025, then fell sharply in Q1 2026

body.text: 2025 full-year gross retail leasing across the top eight cities reached a post-COVID high of 9.21 million sq ft. But Q1 2026 leasing fell to 1.95 million sq ft, down 28% quarter-on-quarter and 10% year-on-year — the opposite direction from the sustained four-year-high framing this section previously carried, per Cushman & Wakefield's Q1 2026 MarketBeat. Grade A/A+ mall vacancy nationally sits at 5.7%/2.6% (Q1 2026), so space remains tight even as leasing activity has cooled. The 2026–28 supply pipeline is 12.7 million sq ft.

realEstate.title: PlayBlue's three target cities are the three most contested markets

body.text: Mumbai (29%), Delhi NCR (24%) and Bengaluru (23%) together took over 75% of H1 2026 retail leasing volume. Domestic brands accounted for 79.1% of that demand. These are precisely PlayBlue's rollout cities, and the competition for space is domestic rather than international.

realEstate.title: High-street rents are rising fastest exactly where a flagship would go

body.text: Mumbai's Linking Road recorded a 22% annual rent increase; Bengaluru's Indiranagar 100 Feet Road 12%; Chennai's Anna Nagar 2nd Avenue 11%; Delhi NCR's Khan Market 9%. Malls took 51.3% of Q2 2026 leasing and main streets 48.7%. Occupiers are competing hard for well-located assets, producing tighter vacancies and firmer rents.

realEstate.title: Experience-driven formats are gaining mall share

body.text: Malls' share of gross leasing rose to 43.1% from 38.9% a year earlier, attributed to consumer preference for experience-driven retail. Supportive of PlayBlue's experiential format thesis — and equally supportive of every other experiential retailer bidding for the same anchor space.
